title: Academic co-authorship is a risky game

affiliations.1: Department of Cancer Biology, Cancer Institute, University College London, London, UK
affiliations.2: Department of Economics, Western Galilee College, Acre, Israel

abstract: Conducting a project with multiple participants is a complex task that involves multiple social, economic, and psychological interactions. Conducting academic research in general and the process of writing an academic manuscript, in particular, is notorious for being challenging to successfully navigate due to the current form of collaboration dynamics common in academia. In this study, we propose a game-theory-based model for a coauthorship writing project in which authors are allowed to raise an ultimatum, blocking the publishment of the manuscript if they do not get more credit for the work. Using the proposed model, we explore the influence of the contribution and utility of publishing the manuscript on the rate one or more authors would gain from raising an ultimatum. Similarly, we show that the project’s duration and the current state have a major impact on this rate, as well as the number of authors. In addition, we examine common student-advisor and colleague-colleague co-authorships scenarios. Our model reveals disturbing results and demonstrates that the current, broadly accepted, academic practices for collaborations are designed in a way that stimulates authors to raise an ultimatum and stopped only by their integrity and not by a systematic design.
summary: Writing a paper with several co-authors involves social, economic and psychological tensions. We built a game-theory model of a co-authored writing project in which any author can raise an ultimatum, blocking publication unless they get more credit. The model shows that each author's contribution, the value of publishing, the project's duration and stage, and the number of authors all strongly affect how often an ultimatum pays off.
key_findings: We model a co-authored writing project as a game in which an author can block publication with an ultimatum to get more credit.
The project's duration, its current state and the number of authors have a major impact on how often raising an ultimatum pays off.
We examine common student-advisor and colleague-colleague co-authorship scenarios.
Current academic collaboration practices encourage ultimatums, which are held back only by authors' integrity rather than by the system's design.
